summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

primary_citations.citation_text: Kan. Stat. Ann. § 38-2223 — Reporting of certain abuse or neglect of children; persons required to report (Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children, ch. 38, art. 22)
Chapter 38 — Minors; Article 22, Revised Kansas Code for Care of Children (child welfare primary)

regulations_applicable.title: Agency 30 - KANSAS DEPARTMENT FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for SRS workers sued for a negligent child abuse investigation preceding a child's death, holding that the reporting and investigation statute creates only a duty to the public at large and that the decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Kansas authority on liability for screening a report out: there is none, absent an independent duty of care.
key_cases.quote: The decision whether to open a file for further investigation is a discretionary function

key_cases.case_name: Burney v. Kansas Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a negligence verdict for a substitute teacher who had been investigated for child abuse, holding that SRS owes no duty to an alleged abuser, that there is no special relationship between the agency and a suspect, and that both the decision whether to open a file and the manner of conducting a child abuse investigation are discretionary functions immune under the Kansas Tort Claims Act.
key_cases.relevance: Kansas law treats the child protection investigation statutes as creating a public duty only, which bars individual negligence claims arising from screening.
key_cases.quote: we hold that in investigating child abuse cases, SRS owes no duty to the alleged abuser

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed judgment for the county, holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a State to protect a child from private violence merely because caseworkers knew of the danger, while noting that a custodial relationship such as state-operated foster care might be different.
key_cases.relevance: Screening a report out or closing it as unfounded creates no federal constitutional liability even if the child is later harmed by a parent.
key_cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

key_cases.case_name: Gloria G. v. State Department of Social & Rehabilitation Services
key_cases.holding: The court reversed a jury verdict against SRS and entered judgment for the agency, holding that SRS's decision to remove a child from a foster home was a discretionary act immune from liability under the discretionary function exception of the Kansas Tort Claims Act, K.S.A. 75-6104(e).
key_cases.relevance: This is the Kansas Supreme Court source of the discretionary-function immunity that the Court of Appeals later extended in Beebe to the decision whether to open a file at all.
key_cases.quote: SRS is immune from liability because the removal of A. from the foster care home by SRS was a discretionary act under K.S.A. 75-6104(e)

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: A later finding is allowed only if a delay is requested by law enforcement, a county or district attorney, the court, or health or mental health professionals, or exceptional circumstances are documented in the case file (DCF PPM 2511 C.). An allowable late finding requires the Child Protection Specialist to enter "Allowable Delay" on the PPS 2011 Case Findings Section IV on or before the case finding due date; if the finding is late for a reason not allowable under PPM 2511 C., the specialist shall document with the finding: "The case finding is delayed due to a non-allowable reason per policy." (DCF PPM 2531 E.)
